## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.50933.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.50933.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This paper showcases the use of ultra-high field (7 Tesla) fMRI for disentangling the feedforward and feedback interactions across the cortical hierarchy underlying perception. The authors perform a detailed quantification of the laminar-specific patters of neural activity in human early visual cortex (areas V1-V3) during motion-based surface segmentation. This allows them to identify a signal component associated with illusory motion perception that is consistent with feedback from a higher-tier cortical area.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Feedback contribution to surface motion perception in the human early visual cortex" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Tobias Donner as the Reviewing Editor and Christian Büchel as the Senior Editor.

The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Tomas Knapen (Reviewer #1); Lars Muckli (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This study investigates the role of feedback in surface motion perception. The authors use high-field (7T) fMRI to distinguish which layers of the early visual cortex are activated by global motion perception of a surface. This study provides new insights into neuronal processes underlying perception of surface motion – an important and ubiquitous perceptual phenomenon. The perception of surfaces is a construction taking into consideration nearby contextual information, in this instance, cues that give rise to perception of surface motion. The main novel contribution lies in the fact that the authors separate center from surface responses, which has not been done in humans before. Reviewers applaud the authors for approaching important aspects of high-resolution fMRI of visual cortex (anatomical segmentation, unwarping, registration, pRF-based retinotopy) with great care and state-of-the-art methodology. However, reviewers also raised a number of substantive concerns, which would need to be addressed in revision.

Essential revisions:

1) Address the negative overall BOLD response.

The responses in the surface region are dominated by a large negative BOLD response. This negative BOLD effect seems to dwarf the cortical depth-dependent results by a factor of around 20. Reviewers wondered whether a less negative BOLD response for the dynamic Pacman condition could be the result of 1) an increase in activity, or 2) a decrease in negative evoked activity.

In general, the physiological basis of negative BOLD is not well understood. Is it possible that activation in the right visual field could cause negative BOLD in the right V1, not because it induces neural activity in right V1 but for haemodynamic reasons (e.g. “blood stealing”) that are not well understood? In this case, given that right visual field stimulation is different in the three different conditions, could there be different amplitudes of negative BOLD in right V1 due to this? In other words: can we assume that any BOLD effect in right V1 is not influenced by neural activity in left V1? This could present a problem in the interpretation of the current results, which would need to be addressed. Also, reviewers thought that the presence of the big negative BOLD response creates a discrepancy in the paper, which focusses on the depth-dependent results.

Reviewers felt the study would benefit substantially from testing whether the depth-dependent results hold even when the sign of the figure response is changed. This could be achieved by manipulating the background and inverting the sign of the figure-related BOLD response – the feedback-related findings should be the same in the different background conditions.

After some discussion, reviewers and Reviewing Editor agreed that you could approach this general issue in one of two ways:

i) You run an additional experiment that repeats the figure segmentation experiment without the textured background, so as to avoid the large negative BOLD response.

ii) You discuss this issue more prominently in the paper, and acknowledge the resulting limitations in terms of interpretation in the Discussion.

While option (i) would be the preferred course of action (allowing for a conclusive answer to this point), we (and reviewers) leave it to you to decide which of those options you choose.

2) Present laminar results in more detail; in particular, show individual subject data.

The depth-dependent results are presented relatively minimalistically and the analysis is done in summary form using linear mixed models. Two specific suggestions for improvement:

a) It seems that he peak of the depth-level BOLD response is shifted towards CSF for V1 relative to V2 and V3. Can the authors also make this point by an analysis that stays a little closer to the data, for example (and this is just an example) by fitting a quadratic function to the depth-level bold responses and showing that the peak indeed shifts upward for V1?

b) Layer-specific fMRI effects are still a challenging field. To improve the interpretation it would be good to show individual results – alignment of the depth layers to the activity – and main effects of profile across subjects (as supplementary figure).

3) Discuss relationship to (discrepancies with) animal physiology.

Similar questions have been addressed with electrophysiological recordings in animals, particularly by Pieter Roelfsema's lab. In the current study, you report that the laminar profile of surface segmentation differs across the different regions of the early visual cortex, with the effect peaking in superficial layers in V1, and in middle layers in V2 and V3. You propose a neural mechanism for these profiles, with top-down feedback targeting the superficial layers of V1, which subsequently target the middle layers of V2 and (directly or indirectly) V3.

These findings differ from effects of surface segmentation using electrophysiology in animals, which report both superficial and deep layers of V1 being involved. Please discuss possible sources of this apparent discrepancy.

4) Address the role of attention.

A similar interpretational problem as with the negative BOLD issue (point 1) arises with the role of attention. Attention has been suggested to have a similar laminar profile (Lawrence et al., 2019). Also note that Akin et al. suggest that the effect reported here is dependent on attention. It seems possible that the current signals do not at all reflect the neural correlate of surface segmentation, but rather only the secondary effect of top-down attention directed at a (perceptually moving) segmented surface? If the reported signal is an exclusively attentional one, rather than the perceptual signal that captured attention, this would change the interpretation quite profoundly.

As with point 1, the most direct way of addressing of this issue would be to run an additional experiment that controls attention more effectively than the current fixation task – either using a more challenging fixation task and showing psychophysically that this puts the stimuli of interest in the "near-absence" of attention (see work by Jochen Braun, Christof Koch, David Heeger, Sang-Hun Lee, and others); or manipulate attentional load parametrically and show that the current signals are (largely) independent of this. the alternative would be to acknowledge this issue and the resulting limitations in terms of interpretability. Again, we leave the decision about the course of action to you; but please note that points 1) and 2) could be addressed in a single experiment.

Thank you for submitting your article "Feedback contribution to surface motion perception in the human early visual cortex" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Tobias Donner as the Reviewing Editor and Christian Büchel as the Senior Editor. The following reviewer has agreed to reveal their identity: Tomas Knapen (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

This is an overall well-conducted high-resolution fMRI study on the cortical mechanisms of visual surface perception. The authors have thoroughly revised their work based on the reviewer comments. Reviewers and Editors feel that most of the comments were addressed adequately, with some additional control data and additional discussion of the interpretation of the effects. This has improved the manuscript. Yet, there do remain some lingering issues, which we feel would need to be addressed more explicitly through textual revision before this paper can be accepted for publication at eLife. We feel the authors should invest more into incorporating the reviewer comments, rather than simply defending their original conclusions.

Revisions for this paper:

1) Relationship with attention.

The authors have opted not to run an additional control experiment, but rather address the potential role of attention in their findings in Discussion. That is fine in principle, but we do find the new paragraph to be unsatisfying and unclear. Perhaps there may be some confusion about the nature of the concern. We realize that attention may play an intricate (perhaps necessary) role in the cortical computation underlying surface segmentation. But that is not the issue here: the issue is whether the reported effects are (i) due to this computation per se (whether or not some form of attention is involved), or (ii) due to a purely secondary effect of attention being drawn to a segmented surface.

This matters for how the results are conceptualized and understood by the broad readership: The first would constitute a specific neural correlate of surface segmentation per se, whereas the second would be a non-specific signature of any form of object perception (compared to no object).

We acknowledge that arbitrating between these two scenarios is generally a hard problem in visual neuroscience; yet, there are a few compelling demonstrations in the literature for doing so. We feel that, without using similar manipulations here, there is just now way of knowing, which of these two scenarios accounts for the current results. Future experiments will be needed to pinpoint this.

These points, and in particular the two possible scenarios, should be made explicit in the new Discussion paragraph.

2) Negative BOLD response due to stimulus with textured background.

We remain puzzled by the negative BOLD. Intriguingly, the onset of a whole-field textured background (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) elicits an fMRI response that is comparable in positive amplitude to the negative effects within the stimulus region (Figure 4 and 7). This might indicate that in the main experiment, the textured background causes ongoing positive responses throughout the run, presumably maintained by ongoing micro saccades and fixational instability. Then, the presentation onset of a stimulus has a two-fold effect; it decreases the ongoing response to this background (because it disappears) while also playing the role of an activating stimulus very locally (dark patches in the texture are brighter, whereas light patches are darker, stimulating both on and off visual channels temporarily). In this scenario, the negative response shown in Figure 4 should be seen as a combination of a positive and a negative component, that summed together produce the appearance of a delayed negative response.

If the negative BOLD response is indeed a composite of a positive and negative BOLD response, it would be interesting to see how the laminar effects can perhaps decompose this composite. A laminar analysis conducted on the first and later parts of the response separately may be highly insightful here. We understand that SNR may be insufficient to conclusively accommodate this analysis.

This idea (possibly others) deserves unpacking, over and above the brief hint towards this possibility the authors mention in subsection “Background dependence of the negative response”. The fact that the authors have seen similar responses in other contexts doesn't necessarily speak to mechanism in this case.

3) Relationship/discrepancy with previous animal neurophysiology studies:

The authors state in rebuttal: "Finally, electrophysiological experiments typically measure responses over a time window of only a few hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset (300 ms in case of Self et al., 2013). However, the initial and the sustained response to a surface stimulus can have different laminar profiles in V1 (Maier et al., 2011)."

If anything, this makes the discrepancy more puzzling: sustained responses, which the authors imply are more strongly reflected in the BOLD response, are predominant in the deep, not the middle and superficial layers (Maier et al., 2011; Self et al., 2013). This part of the Discussion needs revision.

4) Possibility of visual cortex effects being the result of top-down feedback to the LGN being fed forward to V1.

The authors seem to simply dismiss this possibility, which we find puzzling; a previous study (Akin et al) showed that the experimental modulation used here affects LGN, and depth dependent profiles as reported here in Figure 3, i.e. mostly middle and superficial activations, seems to be very plausibly in line with the effect arising from the LGN, especially when taking the deep-to-superficial draining vein effects into account. Of course, the authors performed a deconvolution to address drain, but we cannot assume that this got rid of any draining vein effects completely. Again, this alternative explanation is worth discussing, rather than simply dismissing it.

results.result: The study demonstrates depth-resolved fMRI activation patterns consistent with feedback during illusory surface motion perception. In V1, activity peaked at superficial layers (~25% depth), while V2 and V3 showed peaks at intermediate depths (~50% and ~40% respectively). Statistical analysis confirmed significant differences in cortical depth profiles between brain areas (p<0.0001), with superficial peaks significantly more common in V1 than extrastriate cortex (p=0.033).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C59-C63, C68-C70, and C102 provide converging evidence from statistical tests, depth profile measurements, and visual data (Figure 4) showing distinct laminar patterns across V1-V3. The superficial bias in V1 versus intermediate depth peaks in V2/V3 is supported by multiple statistical comparisons with significant p-values and is consistent with anatomical predictions about feedback pathways (C104-C106).

results.result: Widespread negative BOLD responses were observed in the retinotopic representation of the surface interior across all stimulus conditions in V1, V2, and V3, while stimulus edges showed transient positive responses. The edge response preceded the surface response by approximately 2 seconds, and this pattern was consistent across areas, conditions, and subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C74-C77, C82, C155-C156 are supported by multiple figures (Figures 2, 3, 5) and describe a robust, replicated finding. The temporal precedence of edge over surface responses (C76) is quantified and illustrated in Figure 5. The consistency across conditions and subjects (C77) strengthens confidence in this observation.

results.result: Control experiments revealed that the negative BOLD response to the surface interior was critically dependent on the presence of a textured background. When stimuli were presented on a uniform background, both surface interior and edges evoked positive responses. The texture background alone produced a positive response of similar magnitude (~3%) to the negative response observed in the main experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C85-C89, C157-C158, C160-C162, C168 are supported by control experiments illustrated in Figures 6, 7, and supplementary figures. The systematic manipulation of background type (texture vs. uniform) provides strong evidence for the causal role of the textured background in producing negative BOLD responses. Multiple control experiments and a simulation (C161) converge on this interpretation.

results.result: The experimental design isolated top-down feedback effects by keeping the left hemifield stimulus physically identical across conditions while manipulating the right hemifield. Because transcallosal connections are restricted to the vertical meridian and the motion percept was induced without local moving elements, differential activity in the left hemifield representation can be unambiguously attributed to top-down feedback rather than horizontal interactions or interhemispheric imbalances.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45, C47-C48, C97-C101, C129, C131-C133 describe the experimental logic and are supported by anatomical knowledge (C48 with citations), stimulus design specifications, and control analyses (C131-C133, Figure 4—supplement 1). The data directly address potential confounds from interhemispheric imbalances, showing that static and dynamic controls yield equivalent activity in V1/V2 left hemifield representation, while the motion illusion condition differs from both.

results.result: The observed depth-resolved patterns are interpreted as consistent with feedback re-entering V1 at superficial layers, followed by feedforward propagation to V2 and V3. Alternative or additional contributions from subcortical structures (pulvinar, LGN) targeting middle layers of extrastriate cortex are also considered plausible based on anatomical evidence and prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C116 present interpretations and speculations about mechanisms. While the interpretations are grounded in anatomical knowledge (C104-C105, C109 with citations) and prior studies (C103, C111-C114), the authors explicitly acknowledge limitations: 'our data do not permit a direct test of the directionality and precise temporal dynamics of information flow' (C107). The mechanistic claims are plausible but not directly demonstrated by the current data.

results.result: Comparison with prior studies shows that while the current results resemble superficial activity reported in scene completion and attention studies, they differ from deep-layer activity in Kanizsa triangle perception and show distinct patterns from feature-based attention. These differences may reflect distinct feedback mechanisms engaged by different paradigms, though all support re-entrant feedback signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121, C139-C143 compare the current findings with specific prior studies (Kok et al. 2016, Muckli et al. 2015, Lawrence et al. 2019) with appropriate citations. The comparisons are fair and acknowledge both similarities and differences. The interpretation that differences may reflect distinct feedback mechanisms (C120, C142) is appropriately cautious and acknowledges uncertainty (C120: 'could reflect', 'should be investigated further').

results.result: The amplitude of the apparent motion effect was small (~0.3% at peak in V2) compared to overall response strength, consistent with previous studies showing small effect sizes of top-down effects relative to bottom-up effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 accurately characterize the effect size with specific quantification (C125: 'slightly more than 0.3%' in V2) and appropriate comparison to prior work (C124: Kok et al. 2016 reported ~0.12%). The characterization as 'small' is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-5 and is consistent with the general pattern in the literature (C123).

results.result: The ~2 second delay between edge and surface responses is discussed in relation to prior psychophysical and neurophysiological findings suggesting surface filling-in occurs over ~100 ms, computational models of contour-surface interaction, and predictive coding frameworks. The delay may result from competing positive and negative BOLD effects that initially balance before the negative response emerges.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C154 present interpretations of the temporal dynamics with appropriate citations to prior work (C145-C149). However, the mechanistic explanations are speculative (C152-C154 use 'possible', 'may'). The authors acknowledge the challenge: 'the question is whether and how this small temporal difference in neuronal responses translates into a ~2 s difference in BOLD response onset' (C151). The proposed mechanisms are plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: The texture background effect was remarkably strong, producing a 4% signal change (from -3% to +1% BOLD) when switching from texture to uniform background. This magnitude is notable compared to typical visual responses (~0.7-1.4% for contrast-reversing checkerboards in similar studies). The negative BOLD is not due to vascular steal, which does not occur in healthy subjects.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C165 provide specific quantification of the effect magnitude with appropriate comparison to prior work (C165 cites Kok et al. 2016). Claims C166-C167 correctly cite the consensus view on vascular steal with appropriate references. The characterization as 'remarkable' (C164) is justified given the magnitude relative to typical visual responses.

results.result: Discrepancies between the current results (superficial bias in V1) and Self et al. 2013 (superficial and deep layer activity in monkey V1) are discussed in terms of methodological differences: MUA vs. postsynaptic activity measured by fMRI, differences in feedforward drive from stimulus types, behavioral relevance of stimuli, and challenges in comparing neurophysiological timescales (~100 ms) with sustained fMRI responses (>10 s).
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C177 provide a thoughtful discussion of potential reasons for discrepancies with appropriate citations (C171-C174, C176). The discussion acknowledges multiple plausible factors without overstating certainty. The methodological considerations are well-grounded in established knowledge about fMRI (C172) and neurophysiology.

results.result: Spatial deconvolution was employed to correct for the bias introduced by ascending draining veins, which cause BOLD signals to be stronger in superficial layers even when neural activity is deeper. While exact deconvolution parameters are difficult to determine, simulations show the method is relatively robust to parameter variations within physiologically plausible ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C184 describe an important methodological consideration with appropriate citations (C178-C179, C180, C182-C183 cite Marquardt et al. 2018 and other relevant work). The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C181) while providing evidence for robustness (C182-C183). This transparency about methodological uncertainty and validation is appropriate.

results.result: The study provides first evidence that induced motion perception in a surface region far from the motion-inducing stimulus produces small activity increases in the retinotopic representation. Despite negative BOLD responses, perceptual assignment of surface features yielded signal enhancement consistent with other studies, suggesting common mechanisms of surface perception across different displays.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C187, C189, C191 appropriately summarize the main findings with appropriate caveats. C185 correctly identifies novelty ('first evidence'), C186-C187 accurately characterize the unexpected negative BOLD finding, and C189 appropriately contextualizes findings relative to prior work. C191 offers a reasonable synthesis about common mechanisms while acknowledging differences (C190).

results.result: The experimental design used a Pac-Man stimulus (7.5° diameter) with a rotating sector in the right hemifield inducing illusory motion perception of the entire disk, while the left hemifield remained physically constant. Two control conditions (static and dynamic) were included. Stimuli were presented on a textured background in a block design with variable rest periods. Participants performed a central fixation task throughout.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43, C46, C49-C51, C194-C211 provide detailed, internally consistent descriptions of the experimental design with specific parameters. The design is well-documented with figures (Figure 1) and videos (referenced in C97, C203). The methodological advantages are clearly articulated (C46, C49) and logically justified.

results.result: Nine healthy participants (mean age 27.6 years) completed the study with ethical approval. Data were acquired at 7T with 0.8mm isotropic resolution using 3D GE-EPI. Standard preprocessing included motion correction, distortion correction, and GLM analysis with separate predictors for sustained and transient responses. Quality control excluded runs with <70% target detection, resulting in exclusion of one subject.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C193, C219-C228 provide comprehensive methodological details with appropriate citations for software and sequences used. The quality control criteria (C227) are clearly specified and applied (C228). The containerization for reproducibility (C226) is commendable. All essential methodological information is provided.

results.result: Anatomical images were registered to functional data with upsampling to avoid downsampling. Tissue segmentation was performed with FSL FAST and semi-automatically refined. Cortical depth profiles were constructed using volume-preserving parcellation (10 compartments). ROIs were defined in an observer-independent way based on retinotopic mapping (R²>0.15), signal intensity thresholds, and eccentricity criteria (1-3° for center, 3.5-4° for edge). Spatial deconvolution was applied to remove venous bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C229-C243 provide detailed, reproducible methodology with appropriate citations for all software and methods used (C232-C234, C237, C243). The ROI definition approach is quantitative and observer-independent as stated (C236). The criteria are clearly specified (C239-C241) and justified. The spatial deconvolution is appropriately referenced (C243).

results.result: In V2 and V3, the two control conditions showed statistically significant differences in activation patterns and depth profiles (p=0.0491 for depth interaction). In V3 specifically, the dynamic and static controls were not equivalent (p<0.0001), with V3 showing sensitivity to interhemispheric activity differences. The dynamic control was considered superior because it better matched the physical motion in the experimental stimulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67, C134-C136 report specific statistical findings with p-values and provide appropriate interpretation. The conclusion that the dynamic control is superior (C67, C136) is logically justified based on stimulus matching considerations. The finding that V3 differs from V1/V2 in sensitivity to interhemispheric differences (C135) is supported by the statistical analysis (C66, C134).

results.result: At the stimulus edge, differential activation among visual areas was observed (p<0.0001), but there was no evidence for differences in cortical depth profiles between conditions (p=0.46). This lack of depth-dependent differences is likely due to strong feedforward drive from local contrast engaging neurons equally across cortical depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 report statistical findings with appropriate p-values and provide a reasonable interpretation (C73). The interpretation that strong feedforward drive may engage neurons equally across depth is plausible and appropriately presented as likely rather than certain ('likely due to', 'may engage').

results.result: Control experiments with longer stimulus duration (25s vs ~10s) showed that temporal dynamics were similar and that the negative response to the surface center was sustained over long durations. Separate analysis of early and late response phases showed no evidence for temporal differences in laminar activation profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 describe findings from a control experiment (n=5 subjects) illustrated in supplementary figures. The findings support the characterization of the response as sustained rather than transient and show consistency in laminar patterns over time. The control experiment appropriately addresses a potential concern about temporal dynamics.

results.result: Dynamic stimulus parts (rotating Pac-Man mouth and dynamic control wedge) caused positive signal changes in V1, V2, and V3 as expected. The spatial extent of negative signal change was similar across conditions but differed across regions, with increasing blur from V1 to V3, likely due to increasing receptive field sizes in higher-order areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C83-C84 describe expected findings (C81: 'as expected') and provide reasonable interpretation of spatial patterns based on established knowledge about receptive field sizes (C84 with citation to Gattass et al. 1981). The observations are illustrated in Figure 3.

results.result: Temporal dynamics in the texture background condition closely resembled the main experiment (transient positive at edges, sustained delayed negative at surface). With uniform background, responses were positive and sustained for both interior and edges. The temporal shape of edge responses changed with background type. The delay in negative response is unlikely related to motion since it occurs in all conditions, and may be due to slow decrease from elevated baseline or varying physiological contributions to negative BOLD.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 describe findings from control experiments illustrated in Figures 5-6. The inference that delay is unlikely related to motion (C93) is logically supported by consistency across conditions. Claims C94-C96 appropriately present speculative interpretations ('may be due to', 'it is possible') with acknowledgment that more research is needed (C96).

results.result: The experimental design raises questions about potential interhemispheric interactions and attentional contributions. While transcallosal connections and higher-order feedback could affect interhemispheric balance, and attention can cause positive responses at attended locations and negative at unattended locations, the data do not support that these factors drove the observed pattern. However, the fixation task likely permitted minimal attention to the visual field, and it cannot be fully excluded that observations reflect general attentional contributions rather than motion-specific computations.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128, C130, C137-C138, C144 appropriately identify potential confounds with citations (C127-C128), describe the experimental design (C130), and acknowledge limitations in interpretation (C137-C138, C144). The discussion is balanced, acknowledging both what the data do and do not support. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C144: 'cannot fully exclude') is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Control experiments investigated the role of stimulus shape and background by presenting Pac-Man and square stimuli (identical in luminance and area) on either uniform or texture backgrounds. An additional experiment probed response to texture background alone without additional stimulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C218 describe control experiments with clear specifications. The experiments are well-designed to isolate the effects of shape versus background. The descriptions are consistent with figures (Figure 7 and supplements) and provide necessary detail for interpretation.

results.result: Activation maps were projected into visual field space based on population receptive field estimates to facilitate interpretation. Statistical analysis used linear mixed effects models fitted to percent signal change estimates from sustained and transient predictors. Peak positions in cortical depth profiles were analyzed, with peaks in the upper third of gray matter counted as 'superficial'. Chi-squared tests compared the ratio of superficial peaks between areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C244-C250 describe analysis methods with clear rationale (C244 explains why visual field projection is useful) and specific definitions (C249). The statistical approach using mixed effects models (C245-C247) is appropriate for the hierarchical data structure. The peak analysis method (C248-C250) is clearly defined and appropriate for the research question.

results.result: Population receptive field mapping used oriented bars (4 orientations, 8 positions each) with contrast-reversing checkerboard patterns (1.25° width, 1.2 cycles/deg spatial frequency, ~1 luminance contrast, 4 Hz reversal). Each of 32 configurations was presented 12 times for 2.08s in random order, for a total run duration of 832s (400 volumes).
results.evaluation: Claims C251-C256 provide comprehensive, specific parameters for the retinotopic mapping procedure. All essential details are included (stimulus dimensions, spatial frequency, temporal frequency, presentation order, duration). The method is standard and well-documented.

results.result: The introduction establishes that while surface perception has neural correlates in early visual cortex, the role of feedback during surface segmentation remains unknown. Feedback projections target superficial and deep layers, leading to predictions about cortical depth distributions. Previous research has shown mixed results, with some studies claiming no early visual cortex contribution to surface processing, while numerous fMRI and electrophysiology studies demonstrate retinotopic signals. Only a handful of studies have tested layer-specific activity during feedback in surface perception, with complex patterns observed. Separating edge from surface responses is critical since contour responses also involve feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C40 provide appropriate background with extensive citations to establish the research context. The characterization of prior work is accurate and balanced, noting both studies claiming no early visual cortex role (C15) and numerous studies showing retinotopic signals (C16-C17). The identification of gaps in knowledge (C2, C21) appropriately motivates the current study. Critical evaluation of prior work (C36) is fair and constructive.

results.result: A previous non-depth-resolved fMRI study using similar stimuli reported smaller BOLD response to gray figure than textured background, possibly reflecting stronger sensory response to texture. The current study hypothesized that illusory surface motion would be associated with enhanced activity in superficial and/or deep layers compared to controls, consistent with feedback contribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 appropriately cite and interpret prior work (Akin et al. 2014) and clearly state the study hypothesis. The hypothesis (C54) is appropriately framed as speculation ('hypothesized') and is logically derived from anatomical knowledge about feedback projections. The hypothesis is testable and guides the experimental design.

results.result: The study demonstrates the potential of depth-resolved fMRI for addressing questions about perception. Open questions remain about whether neural mechanisms behind negative responses have functional roles in surface perception, and whether different surface features result in distinct depth-resolved patterns suggesting various feedback sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C188, C190 appropriately summarize the methodological contribution (C9) and identify important open questions for future research (C188, C190). These are reasonable conclusions that acknowledge both what was accomplished and what remains uncertain. The identification of open questions is appropriate scientific practice.
